question: The European Union's energy security requires diversification not only of natural gas suppliers but also of its transportation routes, in order to prevent the creation of new geopolitical dependencies.

The Azerbaijan–Georgia–Romania Interconnector (AGRI) plan envisages the transportation of Azerbaijani natural gas via Georgia and the Black Sea to Romania, with liquefaction and regasification, completely bypassing Turkish territory. Although the project has been discussed since 2010 and has been the subject of feasibility studies, it has not yet been implemented.

At the same time, the EU continues to rely on the Southern Gas Corridor, the TANAP section of which passes through Türkiye, strengthening its importance as an energy transit country. The development of an alternative route through the Black Sea could strengthen the EU's strategic autonomy and energy cooperation with Georgia, Romania and Azerbaijan. In view of the above: 1.
Has the Commission assessed the economic and technical viability of the AGRI, as well as its strategic value in reducing dependence on Türkiye as a transit country?
Does the Commission intend to consider financing relevant studies and infrastructure through the Global Gateway, the Connecting Europe Facility or other European financial instruments?
Why has this alternative route not been effectively promoted, despite the declared European aim of diversifying energy routes?
